source.title_on_document: Homogenizing effect of large language models (LLMs) on creative diversity: An empirical comparison of human and ChatGPT writing

paper_design_summary: Three preregistered studies compare archival college admissions essays written by applicants to a private East Coast US university (2018-2022, before ChatGPT) with essays that GPT-4 generated from the same essay prompt, under base, naive-prompt, parameter-modified, and chain-of-thought configurations (2,200 essays in total). No person received AI assistance. Each essay gets a BERT-based semantic-distance score (DSI, 'individual diversity'), and each condition gets a 'diversity growth rate': the slope of collective semantic diversity on the log number of pooled essays (2 to 34).

studies.label: Study 1: human vs base GPT-4 (ChatGPT interface) admissions essays

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned to people. Human essays were randomly sampled from an archive; GPT-4 essays were generated by the authors.
assignment.quote: We compared a set of 100 essays written by humans randomly chosen from submissions between 2018 and 2022 with another set of 100 essays generated using GPT-4.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 2, Section 3.2 (OSF https://osf.io/ywap5/registrations; Study 1 registered July 5, 2023; deviations in Tables S9-S10)

arms.name: Human
arms.description: 100 archival admissions essays written by applicants, randomly chosen from 2018-2022 submissions (Fig. 1: Human n = 100)

arms.name: Base GPT-4
arms.description: 100 essays generated by the authors through the ChatGPT (GPT-4) chat interface, June 24-30, 2023, one new chat session per essay; no human participant (Fig. 1: n = 100)

participants.exclusions: No participants. The archive pool is 49,804 essays after excluding 1,000 essays used in pilot studies (p. 3, Section 3.3.1). Titles and footers of GPT-4 essays were excluded from the text analyzed (p. 5, Section 4.1). The paper counts essays (100 + 100), not people.
participants.who: Authors of the human essays are applicants to a private East Coast university (archival essays, 2018-2022); they were not recruited and did not use AI. The number of distinct applicants is not stated.
participants.country: United States (university location); applicants' countries not stated
participants.quote: We randomly selected human-written essays used in Studies 1–3 from the archival data submitted by applicants to a private East Coast university from 2018 to 2022 before the public launch of ChatGPT.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 via the ChatGPT chat interface (API not accessible at the time)
ai_tool.how_used: AI wrote whole essays on its own. Prompt: 'As a college applicant, please generate my admissions essay of approximately 650 words in response to the following prompt: [Essay Prompt].' (p. 3, Section 3.3.2; p. 5, Section 4.1)

task.description: College admissions essay (about 650 words) answering the prompt: 'As OOOO University is a diverse community, the Admissions Committee would like to know more about you in your words. Please submit a brief essay, either personal or creative, which you feel best describes you.' (p. 3)

outcomes.name: Individual diversity (Divergent Semantic Integration, DSI) of each essay
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: DSI (Johnson et al., 2022): mean cosine distance between all pairs of word embeddings (bert-large-uncased, layers 6 and 7) within one essay, multiplied by 1,000. The paper calls it 'individual diversity' and treats it as the creativity level of an essay (pp. 3-4, Sections 3.4.1-3.4.2). Robustness: Sentence-BERT all-mpnet-base-v2 sentence embeddings, with and without sampling (Fig. S1-S3, Tables S6-S7, supplement not in file). Welch t-test (p. 4, Section 3.5).

contrasts.reported: Human vs Base GPT-4: Mean Difference = 8.95, 95% CI 7.14, 10.76, Cohen's d = 1.38, t(159.89) = 9.75, p < .001. Fig. 1 labels: Human 829.59 (7.92), n = 100; Base GPT-4 820.64 (4.64), n = 100 (parenthesized values unlabeled in the figure).
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 4.2.1; p. 6, Table 1 and Fig. 1

outcomes.name: Diversity growth rate (DGR) of collective diversity
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Collective diversity = DSI of 34 sentences sampled from k pooled essays of one condition, averaged over 5,000 draws, for k = 2 to 34 (33 scores per condition). DGR = slope b on ln(k) from a regression of collective diversity on ln(k), authorship dummies, and interactions; doubling effect = b x ln(2). Slope differences tested post hoc with Holm correction (pp. 4, Sections 3.4.3 and 3.5). Robustness with Sentence-BERT embeddings in Fig. S1-S3, Tables S6-S7 (not in file).

contrasts.reported: Human DGR b = 0.58, 95% CI 0.50, 0.66, doubling effect 0.40, SE 0.04, df 62, t 15.35, p < 0.001; Base GPT-4 b = 0.18, 95% CI 0.11, 0.26, doubling effect 0.13, SE 0.04, df 62, t 4.82, p < 0.001. Difference: b = 0.40, 95% CI = [0.29, 0.50], p < .001 ('about 31% of the diversity growth rate observed for human-written essays').
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 4.2.2; p. 6, Table 2; p. 7, Fig. 2 (pairwise detail in Table S3, not in file)

diversity_detail.metric: Diversity growth rate: slope of collective diversity (mean pairwise cosine distance among word embeddings in 34 sentences sampled from k pooled essays, x 1,000) on ln(k), k = 2 to 34
diversity_detail.computed_over: All word pairs within 34 sentences randomly sampled from k randomly chosen essays of the same condition; 5,000 bootstrap draws per k, averaged
diversity_detail.uncertainty: OLS regression of the 33 collective-diversity scores per condition on ln(k) x authorship (df = 62); per-slope SE, 95% CI, t; post-hoc slope comparisons with Holm-adjusted p
diversity_detail.notes: Higher DGR = less homogenization. Fig. 2 plots collective minus individual diversity.

data_and_code.data_url: https://osf.io/ywap5 (processed data, GPT-4 essays, demographics; human essay text not shared)

eligibility.reason: No person was assigned to or received AI assistance. The paper compares archival human-written admissions essays with essays GPT-4 generated on its own (pp. 3 and 5, Sections 3.3 and 4.1). Counts are essays (200, 400, 1,600), not participants. The outcomes are computed semantic-distance measures on the essays, so the outcome type would qualify, but the design is AI versus human output (context).

one_line_finding: In three preregistered studies of 2,200 admissions essays, GPT-4 essays had lower diversity growth rates than human essays (Study 1: human b = 0.58 vs base GPT-4 b = 0.18; Study 3: 0.62 vs 0.07, CoT 0.31; p. 6, Table 2), including when prompt or parameter changes raised individual-essay DSI to or above human levels (p. 6, Table 1).
open_questions: Table 1 (p. 6) prints the Study 3 CoT-prompted vs Base GPT-4 95% CI as '−1.43, 3.33', which does not match the printed t = 4.90, p_holm < 0.001; possible typo for 1.43. Recorded as printed.

Study 3 random vs diverse human DSI: Table 1 (p. 6) prints Diverse human minus Human = −0.25, t = −0.51, d = −0.04; the text (p. 7, Section 6.2.1) prints 0.25, t(1596) = 0.51, d = 0.04. Fig. 1 levels (829.42 vs 829.17) match the table's sign.
The parenthesized values next to the means in Fig. 1 (p. 6) are not labeled in the figure or note; they look like SDs but the paper does not say so.
The paper does not say whether the human essays used in Studies 1-3 overlap; Studies 2 and 3 report identical human DGR (0.62, 95% CI 0.54, 0.70; Table 2).

The sign convention of the printed DGR slope differences is not stated in the main text (e.g., parameter-modified vs base is described as an increase but printed as b = −0.18); Table S3 in the supplement, not in the file, holds the detail.
Table S7 is cited both for author demographics (p. 3, Section 3.3.1) and for sentence-embedding robustness results (p. 3, Section 3.4.1); the supplement is not in the file.
notes: Design class is ai_vs_human for all three studies: no human participants were recruited or assigned, and no one used AI while writing. Within-paper contrasts among GPT-4 configurations (base, naive prompt, parameter-modified, CoT) are model-only and coded comparison_type 'other'; human-vs-human contrasts (diverse vs random applicants) are also 'other'. In ai_vs_human contrasts I set the GPT-4 condition as treatment and the human condition as control. The paper does not label either outcome as primary; DGR is the paper's headline measure. DSI is coded overall_creativity/automated_score because the paper uses it as an essay's creativity level, although it calls it 'individual diversity' (within one essay, not across people). n_units for DGR outcomes count the collective-diversity scores in the regression (33 per condition; consistent with printed df 62 and 124). ai_available_when_produced is 'mixed' because human essays were written before ChatGPT and AI essays were produced entirely by GPT-4. The markdown conversion gives the Study 3 CoT SD in Fig. 1 as 4.86; the PDF shows 4.88. Supplement (Tables S1-S10, Fig. S1-S3) not available in the files.
